tagline.text: Seven volcanic crater lakes around San Pablo City, Laguna

location.label: Location
location.text: San Pablo City, Laguna (Sampaloc, Bunot, Calibato, Palakpakin, Mohicap, Pandin, Yambo)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500–1,500 (day trip from Manila by public transport, including raft and meals; rough estimate)

children.text: The Seven Lakes of San Pablo are seven volcanic crater lakes scattered around San Pablo City in Laguna. It is an easy day trip from Manila: ride a bamboo raft on Pandin and Yambo, swim at Mohicap, and stroll the shore of Sampaloc, the biggest lake.

The Seven Lakes of San Pablo is the name given to seven lakes spread around San Pablo City in Laguna: Sampaloc, Bunot, Calibato, Palakpakin, Mohicap, Pandin and Yambo. Wikipedia describes them as maar-type craters of the San Pablo Volcanic Field, one of roughly 200 small volcanoes along the Macolod Corridor between Mount Makiling and Mount Banahaw. They formed when groundwater met rising magma and exploded, and the resulting pits filled with water.

The seven lakes differ a great deal in character. Sampaloc, in the middle of the city, is the largest at about 104 hectares and has a lakeside park and cafes. Pandin and Yambo are twin lakes known for clear water and bamboo raft tours, and Mohicap is a lake you reach down a flight of steps and can swim in. Bunot and Palakpakin, on the other hand, are centered on fish pens and angling, so they are mostly places to look at rather than swim. Calibato is said to be the deepest of the seven at about 135 m. Some people try to visit all seven in a day, while many others pick just Pandin, Yambo and Mohicap and take it slowly.

Each lake also has a legend. One says Sampaloc formed when the orchard of a stingy old woman sank. Another says Pandin, cursed never to touch the ground, and her lover Yambo became the twin lakes. Another says the name Bunot comes from a word meaning coconut husk. Treat these as local stories to enjoy while walking around the lakes rather than as fact.

It also helps to know about the environmental problems. According to Wikipedia, illegal settlements, illegal fish pens and commercial structures along the shores increased pollution, and excess feed led to fish kills in the early and late 1990s and in January 2004, when six of the seven lakes were affected. In 2022–2023, the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB), with funding from DOST-PCAARRD, monitored water quality, and the tourism lakes (Pandin, Yambo, Mohicap and Sampaloc) were reported to have satisfactory water quality in the August 2022 measurements. The lakes used for fish farming and fishing had periods when dissolved oxygen exceeded recommended levels. The lakes are a playground but also a livelihood for local people, so please do not leave any trash.

The two lakes are twins separated by a thin strip of land. Pandin covers about 20.5 hectares and is about 63 m deep, while Yambo covers about 28.5 hectares. From the Pandin landing you can cross by bamboo raft or walk to Yambo. Pandin is easy to reach and gets the most visitors. Yambo is described as the least touched of the lakes and has a rope swing.
On Pandin and Yambo you can board a bamboo raft, cross the lake and have a meal on the water. A 2008 guide listed a Pandin bamboo raft at about
and a large floating picnic raft to Yambo at about
(negotiable). Prices change, so check at the landing.

Mohicap is a small lake of about 14.5 hectares. You pass through a garden entrance and walk down 105 steps to the shore. It is often recommended for swimming along with Pandin and Yambo. There are steps to climb back up, so save some energy after your swim.
Calibato is in Barangay Sto. Ángel and, at about 135 m maximum depth, is the deepest of the seven lakes. You follow a short rocky path of about
10 minutes
on foot from the highway, and some visitors say it is good for birdwatching. The rocks are slippery on rainy days, so be careful.

Sampaloc is the largest lake, right behind city hall, with a promenade, cafes, restaurants and places to stay. It is not recommended for swimming, but it is a good place for a sunset walk and a meal. It makes a pleasant last stop for the day. Sampaloc also has its own entry among the registered destinations, where you can read more.

blocks.title: The fish-pen scenery of Bunot and Palakpakin

children.text: Bunot is in Barangay Concepcion, about
4.5 km

from the city proper, with a maximum depth of about 23 m. Palakpakin is a shallow lake with a maximum depth of about 7.5 m, and you can look down on it from a small bridge right beside the road. Both have fish pens, so swimming is not recommended and visits are mostly for photos and sightseeing.

It is reported that the Rotary Club of San Pablo opened hiking trails connecting the lakes in 2005. Mt. Kalisungan and Tayak Hill are known as viewpoints overlooking the lakes, and Mt. Cristóbal can be seen from several of them. The hiking is easy, though some sections are muddy.
It is common to have lunch in San Pablo city proper between lakes. Lakeside restaurants get crowded on weekends, so eat a little early.
Take a Lucena-bound bus via San Pablo from Buendia–Taft in Manila or from Kamias in Quezon City. The 2008 guide expected arrival around
, and with traffic it can take more than 2 hours.
From the San Pablo bus stop, take a tricycle to Bunot Lake first and take some photos. It is close to the city, so it makes a quick visit.
Ride a Nagcarlan-bound jeepney, get off at Sto. Ángel and walk to Calibato Lake. Come back and take a jeepney to the Pandin entrance.
At Pandin, take a raft across to Yambo, enjoy the scenery and lunch, and swim.
Return to the city for a late lunch, then take a tricycle to Palakpakin and Mohicap. At Mohicap, walk down the steps to swim.
Walk along the Sampaloc shore, have dinner, and take a bus back to Manila. The 2008 guide expected arrival in Manila around
Visiting all seven lakes in a day is tight. If you are short of time, pick just Pandin, Yambo, Mohicap and Sampaloc. Jeepney and tricycle fares need to be negotiated, so confirm them before you ride.

items.title: Day trip by private or rental car
items.subtitle: An itinerary with the Nagcarlan Underground Cemetery

children.text: From Manila take SLEX, exit at Calamba, and head toward San Pablo via Los Baños and Bay.
Stop at the Nagcarlan Underground Cemetery, then go to Yambo and Pandin. One blog itinerary saw Yambo first, then Pandin, Calibato, Palakpakin, Mohicap, Bunot and Sampaloc, in that order.
Have lunch by a lake and walk down the 105 steps at Mohicap to see the lake.
Stop at Bunot and Sampaloc, walk along the shore, and head home.
Many one-way streets in San Pablo city have no signs. Keep a map app on and drive slowly.
Take a bus signed "Lucena via San Pablo" from the Buendia–Taft corner or from Kamias in Quezon City (near Cubao).
Without traffic it takes about
2 hours
, and much longer in traffic. The 2008 guide gave the fare as about
, and it seems to have risen since, so confirm when you board.
After you get off in San Pablo, tricycles connect you to each lake. Between lakes you alternate between jeepneys and tricycles.
A 2008 source says a tricycle to Bunot cost about
for four people. It may be more now, so be sure to negotiate.
For Calibato and Pandin, take a Nagcarlan-bound jeepney, get off at Sto. Ángel and walk in. In 2008 the jeepney fare was around
Take SLEX, exit at Calamba, and head toward Los Baños and San Pablo. Allow about
2–3 hours
from Manila.
Driving is faster and more comfortable, but parking at lake entrances can be tight.
The dry season from November to May is the most comfortable time for a lake tour. The paths are less slippery and the water is relatively clear.

In the rainy season (June–October), rocky paths such as the one to Calibato are slippery and the lakes can turn murky. On weekends and during Holy Week, Pandin and Yambo are crowded, so a weekday morning is recommended.

San Pablo city has hotels and guesthouses plus restaurants and cafes by Sampaloc, and on a day trip many people eat lunch in the city. There are reports of cafes, restaurants and places to stay along the Sampaloc promenade, and at Yambo and Pandin there are raft tours where you eat on the water. Prices at specific places change, so check on the spot.
If you stay overnight, base yourself in San Pablo city and add Mount Makiling, the shoe town of Liliw or the Nagcarlan Underground Cemetery the next day. See the related registered destinations.
Swim mainly at Pandin, Yambo and Mohicap. Swimming is not recommended at Bunot and Palakpakin because of the fish pens.
Bring a change of clothes, a towel and a waterproof bag. Restrooms and changing rooms at the lakes can be basic.
Do not try to do everything in one day. Pick three or four lakes and enjoy them slowly.
Agree clearly on the raft fare and route at the Yambo and Pandin landings before you board.
Carry plenty of small bills (₱20 and ₱50). Entrance fees and raft fares are paid in cash.
Tricycle drivers know the lakes well if you ask for directions. Keep a map app on as well.
Sampaloc is in the city center and is a good evening stop, but this lake is covered in more detail in its own entry.
Do not swim in lakes with fish pens. Some lakes have had fish kills and poor water quality, so check local advice on arrival.
The rocky path at Calibato is slippery when it rains. Non-slip shoes are safer than sandals.
Some lakes drop off sharply in depth, so children need life vests and an adult beside them.
Take your trash with you. Pollution of the lakes is already a problem.
San Pablo city lacks one-way street signs, so be careful when driving.
Entrance fees, raft fares and opening hours change from time to time, so confirm the latest information locally.
One of the two most popular twin lakes of the Seven Lakes, centered on bamboo rafts and swimming. See its own registered entry.
The largest of the seven lakes, in the city center. A good place for a lakeside walk and a meal.
A Spanish-era underground cemetery a short drive from San Pablo that many people add to their itinerary. Check opening hours locally.
A town famous for its shoe and slipper shops, a good shopping stop after a lake tour.
